scripts.hook: What have you written about three times this month?
scripts.hook_b: Be honest. You know which one.
cards: What have you written about three times this month?
Write the next page in the second person.
"You were passed over. You wanted it."
scripts.visual: V2 own clip of a notebook under a lamp (tag notebook-lamp), else V1 Slate + grain.
scripts.evidence: Tier 1 review (N07) + Moodius practice
scripts.caption:
A notebook can hold reflection or rumination. The difference often isn't what you write about. It's the angle.

When the same sentence turns up twice, switch from "I" to "you" and write the next paragraph like a calm friend describing it.

What do you keep writing about?

Evidence: review of self-distancing research (Kross & Ayduk, 2017). Practice: Moodius. Full essay "Writing to No One" on the Substack, link in bio.
scripts.first_comment: One word for the thing you keep writing about. No details needed.

scripts.hook: Seneca reviewed his whole day, every night.
scripts.hook_b: Two thousand years old, and still the best ten minutes of the day.
cards: Seneca reviewed his whole day, every night.
Not to put himself on trial.
To see it clearly, then let it go until morning.
Idea: Seneca, On Anger 3.36 · Moodius words
Tonight: what went well, what didn't, one thing for tomorrow.
Full essay on the Substack. Link in bio.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate (series control look).
scripts.evidence: Tier 2 primary text (N30), paraphrased
scripts.caption:
Seneca describes reviewing his entire day each night once the lamp was out, hiding nothing from himself, and sleeping better for it. Not a trial. A review.

What's one thing from today you'd do differently?

Source: Seneca, On Anger 3.36 (paraphrased). Full essay "Writing to No One" on the Substack, link in bio.
scripts.first_comment: One thing from today you'd do differently. Go.

scripts.hook: Whose behaviour took up more of your week than it deserved?
scripts.hook_b: Who got under your skin this week?
cards: Whose behaviour took up more of your week than it deserved?
Some of it is a mirror.
Ask quietly: is there a version of this in me?
If there is, call it a mistake. Not a verdict.
Send this to someone who'll admit theirs.
scripts.visual: V3 still of a reflection in a dark window (tag window-reflection), else V1 + grain.
scripts.evidence: Tier 1 lab studies (N01) + Moodius practice
scripts.caption:
In two lab studies, people told they had a feared trait saw more of it in a stranger, and projecting it seemed to help them deny it in themselves.

That doesn't make every irritation a mirror. It makes it worth a question.

What trait in other people gets to you most?

Evidence: Schimel, Greenberg & Martens (2003). Jung's "shadow" is an interpretive idea, not a tested therapy. Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.
scripts.first_comment: One word: the trait in other people you can't stand.

scripts.hook: Marcus Aurelius, on the people who annoy you:
scripts.hook_b: Marcus Aurelius, on the people who annoy you.
cards: Marcus Aurelius, on the people who annoy you:
"When thou art offended at any man's fault, forthwith turn to thyself."
To find where you do the same thing.
Full essay on the Substack. Link in bio.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate.
scripts.evidence: Tier 2 primary text (Meditations 10.30), opening words verified 21 Oct 2026
scripts.caption:
Eighteen centuries before Jung wrote about projection, Marcus Aurelius gave himself an instruction: when someone's fault offends you, turn to yourself and ask where you go wrong in a similar way.

Who's been your teacher this week, without meaning to be?

Source: Meditations 10.30, tr. George Long. Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.
scripts.first_comment: Who's been an accidental teacher for you lately?

scripts.hook: If you weren't okay, who would know?
scripts.hook_b: Not who would care. Who would actually know.
cards: If you weren't okay, who would know?
Who would notice before you said a word.
For a lot of men, it's a short list.
In 1990, 3% of US men had no close friend. In 2021: 15%.
Being fine alone is a skill. Being reachable is another.
Send this to one name on yours.
scripts.visual: V2 own clip: phone face-down on a table by a lamp (tag phone-table), else V1 + grain.

source.author: Daniel Cox
source.work: The State of American Friendship (Survey Center on American Life)

scripts.evidence: Tier 1 survey (E18), verified 21 Oct 2026 + Moodius reflection
scripts.caption:
Most men aren't lonely in the way headlines describe. They're fine. They have colleagues and a group chat.

The better question is who would know if you weren't.

Who's on your list?

Evidence: Survey Center on American Life (Cox, 2021). Reflection: Moodius. Full essay "The Loneliness of Being Fine" on the Substack, link in bio.
scripts.first_comment: No names needed: how many people are on your list?

scripts.hook: Close friendship takes about 200 hours.
scripts.hook_b: The maths of friendship nobody told you.
cards: That's an evening a week, for a year.
School scheduled it for you. Adult life doesn't.
So put it in the calendar. Same night, every other week.
Study: Hall, J. Soc. Pers. Relationships (2019)
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate (series control look).

source.author: Jeffrey Hall
source.work: How many hours does it take to make a friend? (JSPR 36(4))

scripts.evidence: Tier 1 study (E34), figures verified 21 Oct 2026
scripts.caption:
Jeffrey Hall's research estimated roughly 50 hours to go from acquaintance to casual friend, 90 to friend, and more than 200 to close friend.

Nothing in adult life schedules those hours for you. That's the problem, and the fix.

Who would you give the next 200 to?

Evidence: Hall (2019). Aristotle said the same with salt (Nicomachean Ethics VIII.3). Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.
scripts.first_comment: Who's one person you'd want to spend the 200 hours with?

scripts.hook: Does money make you happier?
scripts.hook_b: Both answers are in the data.
cards:
YES
For most people, a little more with every doubling.

AND NO
You adapt to every raise you get.
The part you control is what the next one is for.
What would your next raise be for?
scripts.visual: V3 brutalist stairwell still (tag stairs), else V1 + grain.

source.author: Killingsworth, Kahneman & Mellers
source.work: Income and emotional well-being: a conflict resolved (PNAS 120(10))

scripts.evidence: Tier 1 adversarial collaboration (N04), verified 21 Oct 2026; adaptation (E33)
scripts.caption:
"Money can't buy happiness" and "only rich people say that" are both wrong in useful ways.

A 2023 paper by former rivals found happiness rises with each doubling of income for most people. And decades of research show we adapt to what we get.

What's your next goal actually for?

Evidence: Killingsworth, Kahneman & Mellers (2023); Brickman et al. (1978). Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.
scripts.first_comment: Finish the sentence: "Enough, for me, is…"

scripts.hook: One of the richest men in Rome, on being poor:
scripts.hook_b: One of Rome's richest men, on being poor.
cards: One of the richest men in Rome, on being poor:
"It is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor."
Or every raise will move it.
Full essay on the Substack. Link in bio.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate.
scripts.evidence: Tier 2 primary text (N28), Gummere wording verified 21 Oct 2026
scripts.caption:
Seneca was one of the wealthiest men in Rome, which makes this line from his second letter harder to dismiss, not easier.

Poverty is partly the gap between what you have and what you want. Raise the second faster than the first and a rich person can feel poor forever.

Have you named your enough?

Source: Seneca, Letters 2.6, tr. Gummere. Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.
scripts.first_comment: Have you ever put a number on "enough"? Yes or no.

scripts.hook: What do you understand about yourself but keep doing anyway?
scripts.hook_b: You already know why you do it. That was never the problem.
cards: What do you understand about yourself but keep doing anyway?
You can explain it in three sentences.
And on Thursday night, you do it again.
Across 47 experiments, behaviour moved about half as far as intention.
Insight isn't the bridge. A plan at the trigger is.
Save this for the next Thursday night.
scripts.visual: V2 own clip of a kitchen at night, light on, nobody in it (tag kitchen-night), else V1 Slate + grain.
scripts.evidence: Tier 1 meta-analysis (N31) + Moodius practice
scripts.caption:
Understanding a pattern changes what you intend. It changes much less of what you do.

In a meta-analysis of 47 experiments, interventions that shifted people's intentions moved their actual behaviour about half as far. Insight is real. It just doesn't reach the moment on its own.

What's the one you keep repeating?

Evidence: Webb & Sheeran (2006). Practice: Moodius. Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.
scripts.first_comment: One word for the mistake you understand best and repeat anyway.

scripts.hook: Do you repeat it because you don't really know better?
scripts.hook_b: Socrates and Aristotle disagreed about why you keep doing it.
cards: Do you repeat it because you don't really know better?

ONE READING
Socrates: nobody does wrong knowingly. You just don't truly know yet.

THE OTHER
Aristotle: you know. The knowledge just isn't awake when you act.
If it's ignorance, learn. If it's habit, plan for the moment.
Idea: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VII · Moodius words
Which one is yours? Tell me below.
scripts.visual: V1 + grain, or V3 stairwell still (tag stairs).
scripts.evidence: Tier 2 primary text (N35), paraphrased; Socrates via Aristotle's report
scripts.caption:
Socrates argued that nobody knowingly does wrong, so repeating a mistake must mean you don't truly understand it. Aristotle thought that was too neat: you can know something and still not have it active in the moment you act.

If Socrates is right, the fix is more understanding. If Aristotle is right, it's a plan for the moment.

Which sounds like you?

Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VII (paraphrased). Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.
scripts.first_comment: Socrates or Aristotle? One word.

scripts.hook: You were given two options for anger. Both fail.
scripts.hook_b: Let it out or keep it in. The research says neither.
cards: You were given two options for anger. Both fail.
Or keep it in. Carry it home.
600 students: venting while thinking about the insult made them angrier and more aggressive.
Anger isn't steam. It's a guard dog. Ask what it's guarding.
Send this to someone told to calm down.
scripts.visual: V2 own clip of a punching bag hanging still in an empty gym (tag bag-still), else V1 + grain.
scripts.evidence: Tier 1 experiment (N38) + Moodius reframe
scripts.caption:
Men tend to get two scripts for anger: let it out, or keep it in.

In a 2002 experiment with 600 students, those who hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who'd insulted them ended up angrier and more aggressive than people who sat quietly. And habitual suppression has its own costs.

The third option is slower: name it, then ask what it's protecting.

Which script were you given?

Evidence: Bushman (2002); Gross & John (2003). Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.
scripts.first_comment: What did your anger guard last time? A boundary, a value, your standing, or something softer?

scripts.hook: Is anger ever the right response?
scripts.hook_b: Two ancient philosophers. Opposite answers about your anger.
cards: Is anger ever the right response?

SENECA
Never. Reason can do anything anger does, without the damage.

ARISTOTLE
Yes. At the right person, to the right degree, for the right reason.
Most anger is the wrong size.
Idea: Seneca, On Anger I · Aristotle, Ethics · Moodius words
Who's right? Comment SENECA or ARISTOTLE.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate (quotes and labels read best clean).
scripts.evidence: Tier 2 primary texts (N39, N40), paraphrased
scripts.caption:
Seneca wrote a whole book against anger: whatever good it seems to do, reason can do better. Aristotle disagreed: being angry at the right person, to the right degree, at the right time and for the right reason is a virtue, and never getting angry at real wrongs is a failing.

You don't have to pick a side to notice where they agree. Most anger, in the moment, is the wrong size.

Which of them are you closer to?

Sources: Seneca, On Anger I; Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics (both paraphrased). Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.
scripts.first_comment: SENECA or ARISTOTLE. And why.

scripts.hook: Everyone calls you when something breaks.
scripts.hook_b: The friend who always picks up rarely gets asked how they are.
cards: Everyone calls you when something breaks.
You know where the jump leads are. You pick up at 2 a.m.
Then someone asks how you are.
"Fine," you say. And ask about them.
Psychologists have a name for caring for others to the exclusion of yourself.
It's linked to self-neglect and finding it hard to accept help.
Being needed isn't the same as being let in.
Send it to the friend who always picks up.
scripts.visual: V2 own clip of a phone lighting up on a dark bedside table (tag phone-table), else V1 + grain.
scripts.evidence: Tier 1 theory paper (N42) and studies (N43); no advice in the essay, per format D
scripts.caption:
Every group has one. The person who drives people to the airport, picks up at 2 a.m., and says "fine" when asked.

Helgeson and Fritz called one version of this unmitigated communion: caring for others to the exclusion of yourself. In their research it was linked to self-neglect, overinvolvement and difficulty accepting help. Ordinary caring wasn't.

Giving isn't the problem. Never receiving is.

Who looks after the one who looks after everyone?

Evidence: Helgeson & Fritz (1998); Fritz & Helgeson (1998). Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.
scripts.first_comment: Tag nobody. Just tell me: when did someone last look after you?

scripts.hook: When did you last let someone help you?
scripts.hook_b: Not a favour you paid back the same day.
cards: When did you last let someone help you?
Not a favour you repaid the same day.
In older couples, giving help was linked to living longer.
Prospective study: Brown et al., Psychological Science (2003)
Giving is good. But if you never receive, people stop offering.
This week: accept one offer you'd normally refuse.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate + grain.
scripts.evidence: Tier 1 prospective study (N41, observational) + Moodius practice
scripts.caption:
Giving is one of the best things a person can do. In a five-year study of older married couples, those who gave practical or emotional support were less likely to die during the study. It's observational, so it can't prove cause.

But there's a version of giving that keeps love out: always helping, never accepting. Eventually people stop offering.

This week, accept one offer you'd usually turn down. Which one will it be?

Evidence: Brown et al. (2003). Practice: Moodius. Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.
scripts.first_comment: What's the smallest offer of help you turned down this month?

scripts.hook: What did your house do with anger?
scripts.hook_b: You learned it before you had words for it.
cards: What did your house do with anger?
Shouting? Silence? Slammed doors? Nothing at all?
Now: what do you do with yours?
Most of what we inherit feels like personality.
It's a default. Defaults can be changed.
Idea: Bowen, family systems theory · Moodius words
Save this. Do it with a sibling.
scripts.visual: V2 own clip of an empty kitchen table with two chairs (tag kitchen-table), else V1 + grain.
scripts.evidence: Interpretive framework (N51, Bowen) + Moodius practice
scripts.caption:
Every family has a way of handling anger, money, affection, conflict and failure. You learned yours before you could name it, which is why it feels like who you are.

Try this: write what your house did with each, then what you do now. Mark each one keep, return or not sure.

Which one would you return?

Practice: Moodius. Full essay "The Things We Inherit Without Realising" on the Substack, link in bio.
scripts.first_comment: Anger, money, affection, conflict or failure: which one did your family handle worst?

scripts.hook: You catch your father's sigh coming out of your own mouth.
scripts.hook_b: The research on family patterns is darker and more hopeful than you'd think.
cards: You catch your father's sigh coming out of your own mouth.
Researchers have measured how strongly patterns pass down.
Even in the hardest cases, about two in three people didn't repeat them.
Review: Kaufman & Zigler, Am. J. Orthopsychiatry (1987)
What helped: someone in their corner, and an honest account of what happened.
Inherited isn't the same as sentenced.
Send it to someone breaking a pattern.
scripts.visual: V2 own clip of an old family photo album closed on a table, no faces (tag album-closed), else V1 + grain.

source.author: Kaufman & Zigler
source.work: Do abused children become abusive parents? (Am. J. Orthopsychiatry 57(2))

scripts.evidence: Tier 1 review (N46) + AIFS review of protective factors (N50); format D, no advice
scripts.caption:
In the most studied and hardest case, whether people who were maltreated as children go on to maltreat their own, a 1987 review estimated about one in three did. That's a real risk. It also means most didn't.

The people who broke the pattern tended to have someone supportive, a partner or an adult in childhood, and an honest, coherent account of what had happened to them.

What pattern are you breaking?

Evidence: Kaufman & Zigler (1987); Australian Institute of Family Studies review. Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.
scripts.first_comment: You don't have to share it. Just type 'breaking it' if you're working on one.

scripts.hook: The meeting went well. The flat looks right.
scripts.hook_b: Everything went right today. So why does it feel like this?
cards: The meeting went well. The flat looks right.
The photos look like the life you aimed for.
Then the evening goes quiet, and something doesn't add up.
Graduates who reached wealth and image goals weren't happier a year later.
Study: Niemiec, Ryan & Deci, J. Res. Personality (2009)
Those who grew closer to people and grew as people were.
The emptiness isn't ingratitude. It's information.
Send it to someone whose life looks great.
scripts.visual: V3 still of a tidy flat at night, one lamp on, nobody in it (tag flat-night), else V1 + grain.

source.author: Niemiec, Ryan & Deci
source.work: The path taken (J. Research in Personality 43)

scripts.evidence: Tier 1 study (N52, 147 graduates); format D, no advice
scripts.caption:
A life can look right from outside and feel empty from inside.

In one study, 147 graduates who made progress on wealth, fame and image goals didn't report more wellbeing a year later, and showed more signs of stress. Those who made progress on relationships and personal growth did report more.

What would you keep if nobody could see your life from outside?

Evidence: Niemiec, Ryan & Deci (2009), a small, well-educated sample. Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.
scripts.first_comment: When did you last feel full rather than successful?

scripts.hook: Would you be happier living somewhere sunnier?
scripts.hook_b: Why other people's lives always look better than they feel.
cards: Would you be happier living somewhere sunnier?

ONE READING
Obviously. Better weather, better life.

THE OTHER
You'd notice the sun for a month. Then you'd just live there.
Students in California and the Midwest were equally satisfied with life.
We judge lives by what's visible. We live them by what isn't.
What are you judging your life by? Comment.
scripts.visual: V1 + grain (Slate), or V3 window with low winter sun (tag window-sun).

source.author: Schkade & Kahneman
source.work: Does living in California make people happy? (Psych. Science 9(5))

scripts.evidence: Tier 1 study (N53, 1,993 students)
scripts.caption:
Almost 2,000 students in the Midwest and Southern California rated their lives. Everyone expected Californians to be happier. Californians liked their weather a lot more, but their overall life satisfaction was the same.

The researchers called it a focusing illusion: we give the visible, distinctive parts of a life far more weight than they have in the living of it. We do it to our own lives too.

What are you judging yours by?

Evidence: Schkade & Kahneman (1998). Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.
scripts.first_comment: One thing about your life that looks better from outside than it feels.

scripts.hook: Two men at the gym at 6 a.m.
scripts.hook_b: Same gym. Same programme. Only one of them lasts.
cards: Two men at the gym at 6 a.m.

ONE
He wants to be strong for the next forty years.

THE OTHER
He can't stand what he sees in the mirror.
Self-critical people made less progress on their goals, not more.
Which one got up this morning?
scripts.visual: V3 empty gym at dawn, rack and bench, no people (tag gym-dawn), else V1 + grain.
scripts.evidence: Tier 1 prospective studies (N56), correlational
scripts.caption:
Two men, same programme, same alarm. One is building something. The other is serving a sentence.

Across five studies, people higher in self-criticism made less progress on their goals, including less weight loss over six months. It's correlational, but it's the opposite of what the inner critic promises.

Which one is getting up in you?

Evidence: Powers et al. (2011). Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.
scripts.first_comment: Building or serving a sentence? One word.

scripts.hook: Would you talk to a friend the way you talk to yourself?
scripts.hook_b: You'd never talk to a friend the way you talk to yourself.
cards: Would you talk to a friend the way you talk to yourself?
People nudged to be kind to themselves about a weakness…
…were more motivated to fix it, not less.
Tonight: write to yourself the way you'd write to them.
Honest about the problem. Kind about the person.
Save this for the next bad week.
scripts.visual: V2 own clip of a pen and an open letter pad under a lamp (tag letter-lamp), else V1 + grain.
scripts.evidence: Tier 1 experiments (E20; design via secondary summary, check before scheduling) + Moodius practice
scripts.caption:
Most people who are hard on themselves think it's what keeps them going.

In four experiments, people nudged towards self-compassion about a weakness, a mistake or a failed test were more motivated to improve, not less.

Try this tonight: write to yourself about the thing you're trying to change, the way you'd write to a friend who was struggling with it. Honest about the problem, kind about the person.

What would that letter say?

Evidence: Breines & Chen (2012). Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.
scripts.first_comment: What would a friend say to you about the thing you're working on?

scripts.hook: Could you sit alone for 15 minutes with no phone?
scripts.hook_b: Most people haven't sat alone with their thoughts since childhood.
cards: Could you sit alone for 15 minutes with no phone?
In one study, many people chose an electric shock instead.
They'd said beforehand they'd pay to avoid it.
We're not broken. We're out of practice.
scripts.visual: V3 plain chair in an empty room, side light (tag chair-room), else V1 + grain.

source.author: Wilson et al.
source.work: Just think: The challenges of the disengaged mind (Science 345)

scripts.evidence: Tier 1 experiment (N08)
scripts.caption:
In a 2014 study, people sat alone in a room for 15 minutes with nothing to do but think, and a button that gave them a mild electric shock they'd earlier said they would pay to avoid. 67% of men and 25% of women pressed it at least once.

The lesson isn't that thinking is unbearable. It's that most of us are out of practice.

When did you last sit with your own thoughts?

Evidence: Wilson et al. (2014). Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.
scripts.first_comment: Honestly: when did you last spend 15 minutes awake with nothing to fill them?

scripts.hook: The queue has a phone in it. The walk has a podcast.
scripts.hook_b: What 15 minutes of chosen solitude actually does to your mood.
cards: The queue has a phone in it. The walk has a podcast.
The bath has a screen balanced on the edge.
Researchers had people sit alone for 15 minutes, no devices.
Strong feelings dropped. Calm rose. More so when they chose what to think about.
Solitude doesn't make you happier. It turns the volume down.
Send it to someone who never stops.
scripts.visual: V2 own clip of a bench by water at dusk, locked off, no people (tag bench-water), else V1 + grain.

source.author: Nguyen, Ryan & Deci
source.work: Solitude as an approach to affective self-regulation (PSPB 44(1))

scripts.evidence: Tier 1 studies (N58, details verified via BPS Research Digest); format D, no advice
scripts.caption:
Fifteen minutes alone, no phone, no task. Students who did it felt fewer strong emotions afterwards, good and bad, and more calm. The effect was bigger when they chose what to think about. In a diary study, a daily 15 minutes made days less agitated.

Solitude isn't loneliness. It's a short gap in the noise.

Where's your 15 minutes going to be?

Evidence: Nguyen, Ryan & Deci (2018). Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.
scripts.first_comment: Where could you find 15 quiet minutes tomorrow?

scripts.hook: Nobody sees the washing-up at 11 p.m.
scripts.hook_b: Character isn't built in the big moments.
cards: Nobody sees the washing-up at 11 p.m.
Or the extra rep. Or the half-truth in a text.
That's where most of a man gets built.
We become builders by building. Just by doing just things.
Idea: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II · Moodius words
Strength isn't the big moment. It's the unseen repetition.
Do one small thing tonight. Tell nobody.
scripts.visual: V2 own clip of a kitchen sink at night, tap running, no hands (tag sink-night), else V1 + grain.
scripts.evidence: Tier 2 primary text (N36), paraphrased
scripts.caption:
We imagine character is decided in big moments. Aristotle thought it was laid down in small, repeated ones: we become builders by building, and just by doing just things.

Most of those repetitions happen when nobody's watching. That's not time off from who you are. It's where you're being made.

What's one small thing you could do tonight and tell nobody?

Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II (paraphrased). Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.
scripts.first_comment: One word: the quality you're building when nobody's watching.

scripts.hook: Who's watching when nobody's watching?
scripts.hook_b: Nobody's watching. Except you, and you're not neutral.
cards: You are. And you take notes.
We often learn who we are by watching what we do.
Keep a promise nobody knew about, and you hand yourself evidence.
Break one, and you hand yourself that too.
Save this. Give yourself better evidence.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate + grain.
scripts.evidence: Tier 3 theory (N59), limits noted in the essay
scripts.caption:
Daryl Bem proposed that we often learn what we feel and value the same way other people do: by watching what we do and working backwards.

So the promises you keep to yourself in private do two things. They build a habit, and they give you evidence about who you are.

What evidence did you give yourself today?

Theory: Bem (1972), self-perception; it applies most when our sense of ourselves is unclear. Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.
scripts.first_comment: What's one promise to yourself you kept this week that nobody knows about?
